definition: To communicate an idea, feeling, or message so that someone else understands it.
example: A single raised eyebrow can convey more doubt than a long speech.
nuance: To express something is to put it out, but to convey it means the meaning actually reaches someone. Don't confuse it with convene, which means to gather.
prompt: A coach writes a short note to a nervous team before the final game.
options: The coach chose a few warm words to convey her confidence in every player.
The coach will convey the whole team in the gym at noon for a meeting.
The coach conveyed her worries by locking the note in a drawer no one ever opens.
The coach conveyed the players to stop worrying, and every one of them agreed.
reasons: Carefully chosen words carry the coach's belief over to the team.
This mixes up convey with convene. Gathering people is not passing along a message.
A hidden note reaches no one, so nothing gets communicated.
This mixes up convey with convince. You convey an idea, not a person to an action.

practice.prompt: A museum guide explains an old painting to a group of students.
options: The guide mumbled so quietly that she conveyed the painting's history to every student in the back row.
The students conveyed about the painting for ten minutes after the tour ended.
The guide pointed out the dark storm clouds the artist used to convey a sense of dread.
The guide conveyed the room slowly, looking for any student who had wandered off.
reasons: Words nobody can hear never reach the listeners, so the history wasn't passed along.
The verb needs a message as its object. It cannot simply mean chatting about a topic.
The clouds are a visual way of getting a feeling across to viewers.
This mixes up convey with survey. Scanning a room is not communicating anything.
